home-remodeling.local_heading: Built for towers, not just houses
intro_paragraphs: Brickell's housing stock runs vertical. The early-eighties bayfront towers, The Palace, Atlantis, and Villa Regina among them, hold generous floor plates with dated bones: enclosed kitchens, dropped ceilings, decades-old risers. Bristol Tower and the Brickell Key buildings added nineties layouts that feel roomy but tired, while newer deliveries like Brickell Flatiron and Una arrive polished yet still get personalized. Owners here routinely buy for the view and the square footage, then take the unit to bare slab and start over. Add the townhomes on Brickell's western streets toward The Roads, platted by Mary Brickell in 1922, and you have a remodeling market unlike anywhere else in Miami.

Permits here run through the City of Miami Building Department, and in a tower that is only half the paperwork. Your association will want a full renovation package: signed and sealed drawings, certificates of insurance, contractor registration, freight elevator reservations, and a schedule that respects the building's working-hour windows. Units from the seventies and eighties often need an asbestos survey before demolition can start. And with many older towers now moving through Florida's milestone inspections and structural integrity reserve studies, boards read renovation plans more carefully than they used to. We prepare packages that pass on the first read.

PGX Builders Group has spent more than 20 years building in South Florida, with 150-plus remodels and additions delivered, and high-rise work rewards our habits: a fixed written scope before demolition, a supervisor on site daily, and finish protection that extends past your front door into the corridor your neighbors use. We keep the freight elevator schedule sacred, keep property managers informed, and close out every permit with inspections signed. One accountable team from the first walk-through to the warranty. Estimate, contract, build, done.

faqs.q: Do I need a City of Miami permit to remodel my Brickell condo?
faqs.a: For anything beyond paint and decor, almost certainly yes. Moving walls, electrical, plumbing, and HVAC work all require permits from the City of Miami Building Department, pulled by a licensed contractor with signed and sealed drawings where the scope demands them. Association approval is a separate track with its own requirements. Unpermitted work surfaces at resale and in building records, and in the current inspection climate it is not worth the shortcut.

faqs.q: How long does association approval take in a Brickell tower?
faqs.a: It varies more by building than by project. Some management offices approve a complete package in a couple of weeks; others hold applications for a monthly board or architectural review cycle. The variable you control is completeness: drawings, insurance certificates, contractor license, and schedule submitted together, formatted the way the building asks. We run city permitting in parallel so the two clocks overlap instead of stacking.

faqs.q: Can I live in my unit during a full remodel?
faqs.a: For a true gut renovation, honestly, no. Most Brickell buildings would not let you try anyway, since demolition, dust control, and daily noise windows make the unit unlivable for weeks at a stretch. For phased or partial remodels we can sometimes sequence the work to keep a bedroom and bathroom functional. We will tell you which situation you are in before contracts are signed, not after.

faqs.q: What does a high-end condo remodel in Brickell cost?
faqs.a: It depends on scope, finish level, and how much of the unit's mechanical systems come with you. A full gut with custom millwork, stone, and new MEP runs several times the cost of a cosmetic refresh, and tower logistics add real labor hours that ground-floor work never sees. We are not the cheapest bid in Brickell and do not try to be. We price the job completely, in writing, before we start.

faqs.q: My building is going through its milestone inspection. Can I still remodel?
faqs.a: Usually yes, and sometimes it is the smart moment. If the association is planning structural or plumbing riser work, coordinating your renovation around it avoids opening finished ceilings twice. Boards in milestone or reserve-study mode do scrutinize renovation plans harder, so clean engineering and complete documents matter more than ever. We have worked in buildings mid-inspection and know how to keep your project off the board's worry list.

kitchen-remodeling.title: Kitchen Remodeling for Brickell Condos, Miami | PGX Builders
kitchen-remodeling.meta_description: Custom kitchens for Brickell towers and townhomes: open-plan conversions, custom cabinetry, stone, City of Miami permits. Estimates at (786) 273-2524.
kitchen-remodeling.hero_sub: Custom cabinetry, stone counters, and open-plan conversions for Brickell kitchens, from bayfront towers to Roads-edge townhomes. Fully permitted, association-approved, and supervised daily by licensed general contractor PGX Builders Group, CGC1539072.
intro_paragraphs: Most Brickell towers built before the mid-nineties came with the kitchen walled off in its own little room, back when a bay view apparently was not something a cook needed. Owners at The Palace, Villa Regina, Bristol Tower, and across Brickell Key have been correcting that ever since: removing the enclosure, adding an island, and letting the kitchen join the living space and the skyline. In newer buildings like Brickell Flatiron and the Rise and Reach towers at Brickell City Centre, the work shifts to upgrading developer-spec cabinetry and stone into something chosen rather than issued.

Kitchen work in Brickell means permits from the City of Miami Building Department for the electrical, plumbing, and wall changes, plus your association's approval before a hammer swings. Tower rules shape the design more than most owners expect: ventilation is usually recirculating or tied to existing building exhaust, gas is rare above the ground floor so induction rules the range, and relocating a sink is governed by where the building's risers actually run. None of this kills a great kitchen. It just means the layout should be designed by people who have read your building's rules first.

Our kitchens are measured twice, once for the drawings and again after demolition, because a forty-year-old slab is never as flat as the plans claim. Cabinetry is built to those field numbers, stone is templated on site, and slabs are chosen at the yard partly for beauty and partly for whether they fit the freight elevator. PGX runs one written scope, one schedule, and daily supervision from demo to final inspection, with lobby and corridor protection your neighbors will appreciate. Twenty-plus years in South Florida taught us that logistics are half of luxury.

faqs.q: Can I remove the wall around my kitchen in an older Brickell tower?
faqs.a: In most units, yes. The enclosure walls in eighties and nineties towers are usually partitions rather than structure, but an engineer confirms that before anyone cuts, and occasionally a column or riser chase hides inside one. The work needs City of Miami permits and association sign-off, and the payoff is dramatic: the kitchen, the living room, and the bay finally in one continuous room.

faqs.q: Can I move my kitchen to a different part of the unit?
faqs.a: Sometimes, and it is the first thing we check against your building's plumbing risers and slab construction. Short relocations along the same wet wall are usually straightforward; moving a kitchen across the unit means pump systems or raised floors and an association conversation, and the cost climbs fast. We will tell you plainly whether the move is worth it or whether a smarter layout in place gets you more.

faqs.q: Do Brickell buildings allow gas ranges?
faqs.a: Very few towers do. Most Brickell high-rises are all-electric above the lobby, which is why induction has become the standard in serious condo kitchens here. Modern induction outperforms most residential gas burners anyway, and it keeps the association and the fire code happy. In the townhomes on Brickell's western streets, where gas service exists, a gas range is back on the menu.

faqs.q: How long does a Brickell condo kitchen remodel take?
faqs.a: Once demolition starts, a full kitchen typically runs a few months rather than a few weeks. Custom cabinetry lead times, stone fabrication, inspections, and building work-hour windows all set the tempo, and the longer runway comes before the start: association approval and City of Miami permits. We sequence orders so materials arrive when the site is ready for them, not before, and the schedule is written into your contract.

faqs.q: What should I budget for a high-end kitchen here?
faqs.a: Custom cabinetry and natural stone put a Brickell kitchen well into serious-investment territory, and tower logistics add labor that a suburban kitchen never needs. Rather than quote a misleading number, we walk the unit, agree on a scope, and put a fixed price in writing. If a budget has a ceiling, say so early. We would rather design to it than surprise you.

bathroom-remodeling.hero_sub: Primary bath renovations for Brickell towers and townhomes: frameless showers, freestanding tubs, stone, and waterproofing treated as the main event. Permitted with the City of Miami and supervised daily. Lic. CGC1539072.
bathroom-remodeling.local_heading: Waterproofing is the luxury nobody sees
intro_paragraphs: The primary baths in Brickell's eighties and nineties towers were built compartmentalized and beige: a tub deck here, a bidet room there, original tile throughout. Owners at Santa Maria, Bristol Tower, and across Brickell Key now rebuild them as open suites, with frameless glass showers, freestanding tubs set where the view earns them, book-matched stone, and vanities with actual storage. In the newer towers, the upgrade is from builder-standard to bespoke. Either way, a Brickell bathroom remodel is really two projects: the one you see, and the waterproofing underneath it that protects the unit below yours.

Bathroom work in Brickell needs City of Miami permits for plumbing and electrical, inspections that include the shower pan, and association approval before any of it. Building rules matter here more than anywhere: most towers restrict moving wet areas beyond their original footprint, hard flooring triggers sound-rated underlayment requirements, and older units can require an asbestos check before demolition. And because every bathroom in a tower sits above somebody's ceiling, associations increasingly ask exactly how yours will be waterproofed. We consider that a fair question with a documented answer.

PGX builds bathrooms in the order that prevents problems: substrate corrected, membranes installed and flood-tested, inspections passed, and only then the stone and glass everyone came for. A supervisor checks the site daily, finishes are protected from trade to trade, and the paperwork, from permits to product approvals, is closed out and handed over. After 20-plus years and more than 150 South Florida remodels, we can say the expensive bathroom failures are almost never the tile. They are the shortcuts under it, which is why we refuse to take any.

faqs.q: Can I move or add a bathroom in my Brickell condo?
faqs.a: Adding or relocating a bathroom depends on your building's plumbing risers and its rules. Many Brickell associations limit wet areas to their original footprint precisely because drainage, venting, and leaks below are building-wide concerns. Where the risers cooperate, we have added baths with engineering the board could approve. Where they do not, we say so at the walk-through and design the best bathroom the footprint allows.

faqs.q: What does high-rise waterproofing involve that a house doesn't?
faqs.a: Stakes, mostly. In a house a failed pan ruins your own hallway; in a tower it ruins your downstairs neighbor's ceiling, art, and patience, and the claim comes with an association attached. So we treat membranes, pan tests, and penetration sealing as documented steps: installed, flooded, verified, photographed, then tiled. It is slower by a few days and cheaper than any alternative by orders of magnitude.

faqs.q: Can I get a curbless shower on a concrete slab?
faqs.a: Often, yes. It takes recessing the pan into the topping slab or raising the surrounding floor, and which option works depends on your building's slab construction and sound-underlayment rules. Where neither is practical we detail a low-profile curb that reads nearly flush. This is exactly the kind of question we answer during the walk-through with a tape measure, not a guess.

faqs.q: Do I need permits for a bathroom remodel in Brickell?
faqs.a: Yes. Plumbing, electrical, and any wall changes require permits from the City of Miami Building Department, with inspections along the way, and your association will require its own approval package with insurance certificates and contractor registration. Tile-only cosmetic refreshes may be lighter on paperwork, but most real bathroom remodels touch regulated systems. We handle both tracks and keep copies of everything for your records and resale.

faqs.q: How long will my bathroom be out of service?
faqs.a: A full primary bath in a Brickell tower generally runs a couple of months of on-site work once approvals are in hand: demolition, rough-in, inspections, waterproofing with its flood test, then tile, stone, and glass, all inside building work-hour windows. Guest baths run shorter. We stage the schedule so a second bathroom stays functional whenever the unit has one, and we put the dates in writing.

home-additions.local_heading: More space without leaving the building
intro_paragraphs: Brickell ran out of empty land a long time ago, so adding square footage here takes creativity. The classic move is sideways: buy the unit next door and combine the two, a strategy owners have used in the generously built towers of the eighties and nineties and across Brickell Key. On the low-rise western streets near The Roads, townhomes and single-family homes still take conventional additions, whether a rear extension, a second story, or a garage that becomes livable space. Both versions are structural work in disguise, and both reward a contractor who starts with engineering instead of optimism.

A unit combination means cutting an opening through a demising wall, which involves a structural engineer, signed and sealed drawings, City of Miami Building Department permits, and your association's blessing, often at board level, since the wall you are opening belongs partly to the building. With many towers now in Florida's milestone-inspection and reserve-study era, boards want to see clean load calculations before approving anything structural, and we agree with them. Townhome additions run on a different track: Miami 21 zoning setbacks, HVHZ-rated openings, and foundations and tie beams designed for the load above.

PGX approaches additions the way lenders approach money: nothing moves without documents. You get a fixed written scope, engineering coordinated under one roof, and a supervisor on site daily while the structure is open, which is the phase where improvisation costs the most. In combined units we plan the mechanical merge properly, so two of everything becomes one system that makes sense. More than 150 South Florida remodels and additions have taught us where these projects go wrong, and our job is to make yours uneventful.

faqs.q: Can I combine two condo units in Brickell?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is the most common form of addition in the neighborhood. The process runs through a structural engineer, the City of Miami Building Department, and your association, which typically must approve any cut into a demising wall. Some buildings also require the combined unit to be documented for tax and title purposes. Done correctly, the result lives like one home and appraises like one; done casually, it haunts every future sale.

faqs.q: Can I enclose my balcony to gain interior space?
faqs.a: In most Brickell towers, no. Balconies are usually limited common elements whose exterior appearance the association controls, and enclosing one changes the building envelope in ways boards and the city rarely approve. We would rather tell you that at the first meeting than after a deposit. Where buildings do permit glazed enclosures under a building-wide standard, we build them to that standard, permitted and hurricane-rated.

faqs.q: Can I add a second story to my Brickell townhome?
faqs.a: Structurally, many of the low-rise homes on Brickell's western streets can take one, but the real answers live in Miami 21 zoning, meaning height, setbacks, and lot coverage, and in what your foundation was built to carry. We start with a zoning review and a structural assessment before anyone falls in love with drawings. If the numbers work, a second story is often the best value per square foot in the neighborhood.

faqs.q: How long does a unit combination take?
faqs.a: Plan on a longer runway than a standard remodel: association and board approval, engineering, and City of Miami permitting all precede demolition, and the construction itself resembles a full gut of both units plus structural work between them. Total timelines commonly run the better part of a year from first drawings to final inspection. We publish the schedule in your contract and manage it weekly, which is how it stays a schedule.

faqs.q: Is combining units worth it financially?
faqs.a: We build rather than appraise, so we will not promise resale math. What we can say: large combined residences with coherent layouts are scarce in Brickell towers, and scarcity has been kind to them, while badly merged units that still feel like two apartments are a harder story. The construction quality of the merge, one mechanical system and no awkward seams, is what separates the two outcomes. That part we control.

outdoor-living.local_heading: The terrace is the backyard here
intro_paragraphs: In Brickell, outdoor living happens off the ground. Wraparound terraces at Santa Maria and Four Seasons Residences, deep balconies along Brickell Bay Drive, rooftop decks on the townhomes near The Roads: these are the neighborhood's backyards, and owners treat them accordingly, with porcelain pavers, summer kitchens where the rules allow, planters, lighting, and furniture that shrugs off August. Few square feet in Brickell work harder than a terrace with a bay view. Most of them are still finished like builder-grade afterthoughts, which is the gap we fill.

Exterior work in a tower comes with structure attached. Balcony slabs and railings are generally building elements under association control, so the line between what you may renovate and what the building maintains gets drawn early, in writing. Electrical, plumbing, and anything fixed in place needs City of Miami permits, and anything that could meet wind needs to be rated for Miami-Dade's high-velocity hurricane zone. This is not the place for a bolted-down pergola of unknown origin. On townhome lots, driveways, stucco, impact openings, and re-roof coordination round out the exterior scope.

We build outdoor spaces for the Brickell climate rather than the catalog photo: marine-grade fixtures because salt air is patient, drainage that assumes sideways rain, membranes protected during construction because your terrace is somebody's roof. Where associations require engineer review of terrace loads or attachments, we arrive with the calculations done. Crews are discreet, protection extends through the lobby, and the project ends with permits closed and a terrace that looks better in year five than most look on day one. That is the PGX version of outdoor living.

faqs.q: Can I put a summer kitchen on my Brickell balcony?
faqs.a: It depends on your building. Many towers prohibit open flame entirely, which rules out gas grills but leaves room for serious electric setups, from built-in electric grills to refrigeration and sinks where plumbing can reach. Larger terraces in some buildings have approved fuller kitchens with association and city sign-off. We read your building's rules before designing anything, so the kitchen we draw is one you will actually be allowed to build.

faqs.q: Who is responsible for my balcony, me or the association?
faqs.a: Typically the structure, meaning slab, railings, and waterproofing, belongs to the building, while your finishes and furnishings belong to you, but the exact split lives in your condo documents and varies by association. It matters because Florida's milestone-inspection era has put balcony structures under real scrutiny, and renovation plans that respect the boundary get approved faster. We establish that line with your association in writing before pricing the work.

faqs.q: What flooring holds up on a bay-facing terrace?
faqs.a: Porcelain pavers are the Brickell workhorse: dense, colorfast, salt-indifferent, and installable on pedestals that protect the membrane and keep drainage working. Natural stone can be beautiful out here but demands sealing discipline, and timber decking needs honest maintenance expectations in this sun. Whatever the surface, weight limits and wind exposure get checked first, since a terrace forty floors up is not the place to discover a paver is a projectile.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for terrace or balcony work?
faqs.a: Cosmetic changes like furniture and planters, no. Electrical, plumbing, anything structurally attached, and most fixed installations, yes, through the City of Miami Building Department alongside your association's approval. Wind-rated attachment matters as much as the permit itself in Miami-Dade's high-velocity hurricane zone. It is unglamorous paperwork, and it is also what stands between your pergola and your neighbor's window in a named storm.

faqs.q: When is the best time of year for exterior work in Brickell?
faqs.a: The dry season, roughly November through April, is friendliest for roofing, stucco, painting, and terrace waterproofing, with less rain and fewer weather delays. Summer work is entirely doable with smart sequencing; we simply schedule moisture-sensitive steps around the afternoon storm pattern. The real calendar constraint is often your building's elevator and approval queue, so starting the paperwork a season early is the most useful move an owner can make.

intro_paragraphs: Brickell permit problems usually arrive with the deed. A kitchen was opened up in a Brickell Avenue tower two owners ago, a bathroom moved in a Brickell Key unit, glass swapped on a West Brickell townhome over a long weekend, and somewhere in that history a permit was pulled and never finalized, or never pulled at all. None of it shows at a showing. All of it shows in the city's permit record, which is exactly what a title company or a lender's underwriter reads before a Brickell closing funds. The owner inherits that file along with the view.

Brickell is City of Miami, so permits are applied for, reviewed and inspected by the City of Miami Building Department at Miami Riverside Center on Southwest 2nd Avenue, filed electronically through the city's iBuild portal. Zoning questions run through Miami 21. Windows, doors and roofing need current Miami-Dade product approvals, because the county sits entirely inside the High-Velocity Hurricane Zone. Buildings other than houses and duplexes carry county recertification, which now begins earlier than the old forty-year mark, and condominium buildings of three habitable stories and up carry milestone inspections and structural integrity reserve studies on top of it.

PGX Builders Group has spent more than 20 years building in South Florida, with 150-plus remodels and additions delivered and every one of them permitted and inspected. We pull permits under our own license, CGC1539072, and bring in the engineer, architect or product documentation a Brickell submittal needs rather than leaving an owner to assemble a package alone. The written scope comes before demolition. A supervisor is on site every day the job moves. Inspections are met by someone who can answer for the work, and the file is not finished until the record reads closed.

scope_items.desc: Complete applications through the city's iBuild portal, drawings and calculations in the first submittal, filed on the same clock as the renovation package your board wants.

scope_items.name: HVHZ product approvals
scope_items.desc: Impact glass, doors and roof assemblies specified with current Miami-Dade approvals and installed to the documented anchorage, because the inspector reads the paperwork against the opening.

scope_items.name: Inspections met in order
scope_items.desc: Rough-in, framing and final inspections booked in the right sequence and attended by the supervisor who built the work, not by a phone number on a form.

scope_items.name: Recertification and milestone repairs
scope_items.desc: Concrete restoration, balcony and railing work, waterproofing and electrical corrections called for by an engineer's report, permitted and closed out around the building's access rules.

faqs.q: There is an open permit on my Brickell condo from a previous owner. What now?
faqs.a: First we read the record at the City of Miami Building Department and establish what the permit covered and how far it got. Sometimes the work was finished and only the final inspection was missed. Sometimes it was built differently, and the honest route is a revision or a new permit. In a tower, add board approval and an elevator booking to the sequence. It runs in weeks rather than days, so start it before a closing date, not after one.

faqs.q: Who issues building permits for Brickell, the city or Miami-Dade County?
faqs.a: Brickell sits inside city limits, so the City of Miami Building Department issues and inspects, with applications filed through iBuild and zoning governed by Miami 21. Miami-Dade County sits above the city too: its Board of Rules and Appeals oversees code administration countywide, county Product Control approves your windows, doors and roofing, and recertification reaches buildings by age. Designated historic sites and the archaeological zones along the bayfront and the Miami River add a Historic and Environmental Preservation Board layer, though most unit work never touches it.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to replace impact windows in a Brickell tower?
faqs.a: Yes, and the paperwork matters as much as the glass. Glazing and doors need current Miami-Dade product approvals because all of Brickell is in the High-Velocity Hurricane Zone, and the installation has to match the anchorage method in that approval. Your association will also hold you to the building standard for frame color and glass tint. Unpermitted window swaps are one of the most common findings we clean up, usually years later, usually under someone else's deadline.

faqs.q: Our building is in milestone inspection. Can PGX do the repair work?
faqs.a: Yes. We do not sign the report, because that belongs to your engineer or architect, but we build what it calls for: concrete restoration, balcony and railing repairs, waterproofing, electrical corrections, and the permits and inspections that close each item out. We work to your engineer of record, the association's access rules, and the freight elevator calendar, and we keep the board's documentation current as items are signed off.

faqs.q: What does it cost to fix a permit problem in Brickell?
faqs.a: It depends on what the record shows and how much has to be opened up to prove it. A missed final inspection is a modest exercise. A wall built without a permit, or a plumbing riser that needs a test, is a project. City fees belong to the city and we pass them through at cost. Our part is priced from a written scope after we have read the file, never guessed at over the phone.
